sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights; through it, each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same (for a typical patient from about 21% at 0 to about 85% at 2 vessels), and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises the risk to about 59%.

Higher resting blood pressure (about 12% at 110 mm Hg to about 38% at 155 mm Hg), higher cholesterol (about 14% at 193 mg/dL to about 36% at 308 mg/dL) and older age (about 15% at 42 to about 26% at 66 years) raise it steadily, and chest pain on exercise raises it to about 33%, an abnormal resting ECG to about 32% and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 27%.

Compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina lowers it to about 2%, non-anginal chest pain to about 4% and atypical angina to about 7%; being a woman lowers it to about 2%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 9%, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 25% at 118 to about 18% at 175 beats per minute.

Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 to 17): a thallium result coded 4 raises the risk to about 78%, while a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 11% and a downsloping ST segment to about 14%.
This part combines two parts, an ischaemia score and a high blood pressure gate, with fasting blood sugar, not as a simple sum.

Through it, ST depression on exercise adds to the predicted risk only once it rises above about 1.3 mm, in an uneven way across patients: for a typical patient with such a fold, from about 31% to about 84%, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

ST depression raises the risk far more with a normal resting ECG (for a typical patient from about 21% to about 74%, against about 32% to about 34% otherwise) and with a maximum heart rate at or below 152 beats per minute (about 23% to about 90%, against about 19% to about 51%), in an uneven way across patients.

Resting blood pressure above about 140 mm Hg lowers the risk through it, mostly in a jump around 140 mm Hg, but for patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less and patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan in stages: for the typical patient it acts on, from above 99% to about 91%, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

This small part adds a fixed amount for the 209 of 242 training patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less (for its typical patient from about 17% without it to about 20% with it), so fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL takes a typical patient from about 21% to about 18% through it.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results) the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 21%; it is the sum of three parts: a weighted sum of most inputs, an ischaemia part held back by high blood pressure, and a small blood sugar step.

This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights; through it, each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same (for a typical patient from about 21% at 0 to about 85% at 2 vessels), and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises the risk to about 59%.

Higher resting blood pressure (about 12% at 110 mm Hg to about 38% at 155 mm Hg), higher cholesterol (about 14% at 193 mg/dL to about 36% at 308 mg/dL) and older age (about 15% at 42 to about 26% at 66 years) raise it steadily, and chest pain on exercise raises it to about 33%, an abnormal resting ECG to about 32% and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 27%.

Compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina lowers it to about 2%, non-anginal chest pain to about 4% and atypical angina to about 7%; being a woman lowers it to about 2%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 9%, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 25% at 118 to about 18% at 175 beats per minute.

Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 to 17): a thallium result coded 4 raises the risk to about 78%, while a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 11% and a downsloping ST segment to about 14%.
This part combines two parts, an ischaemia score and a high blood pressure gate, with fasting blood sugar, not as a simple sum.

Through it, ST depression on exercise adds to the predicted risk only once it rises above about 1.3 mm, in an uneven way across patients: for a typical patient with such a fold, from about 31% to about 84%, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

ST depression raises the risk far more with a normal resting ECG (for a typical patient from about 21% to about 74%, against about 32% to about 34% otherwise) and with a maximum heart rate at or below 152 beats per minute (about 23% to about 90%, against about 19% to about 51%), in an uneven way across patients.

Resting blood pressure above about 140 mm Hg lowers the risk through it, mostly in a jump around 140 mm Hg, but for patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less and patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan in stages: for the typical patient it acts on, from above 99% to about 91%, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

This small part adds a fixed amount for the 209 of 242 training patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less (for its typical patient from about 17% without it to about 20% with it), so fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL takes a typical patient from about 21% to about 18% through it.

parts.name: bp_gated_ischaemia_amplifier
parts.original_hypothesis: Serial gate plus amplifier on ischaemia evidence. (1) Gate: 290 = relu(0.944*ischaemia_score - 1.44*high_bp_gate - 0.897): passes only strong ischaemia evidence (204 > 0.95) not cancelled by high resting BP; active in 71/242 train rows, of which 79% have disease (30% when off). (2) Amplifier: 5615 = 0.248 + 0.998*290 (always active, affine), 2335 = relu(0.893 + 0.898*290 - 1.02*high_bp_gate) (off only for high BP, 27 rows), and 1834 = relu(-1.96 + 0.81*290 + 0.85*2335 + 0.86*5615 + 0.69*fbs:1). With 2335 active and normal fbs, 1834 = relu(2.44*290 - 1.26 - 0.86*high_bp_gate), i.e. threshold 290 > ~0.52; with high fbs the threshold drops below 0 so 1834 is on even when 290 is off (20 rows, at most +0.57 logit). Fitted on train rows with both active: 1834 = 2.40*290 - 1.11. (3) Readout: logit += -0.062*204 + 0.439*290 + 0.747*1834, which on train is about 2.14*290 - 0.81 (resid SD 0.52) when 290 is active and 0.04 +/- 0.17 when off. So the pathway is effectively one steep hinge: risk logit rises ~2 per unit of BP-discounted ischaemia above threshold. Evidence: closed form; train sensitivity (oldpeak dominates, then thal:7, trestbps); local ablations on train: pathway at its mean AUC 0.953 -> 0.926 (log loss 0.283 -> 0.366), no BP inhibition 0.947, no fbs:1 term 0.951, drop 1834 readout 0.939. Pathway logit SD 2.77 vs linear part 3.15.
